title: At the restaurant
goal: Order food and drinks, ask for things politely, and understand the difference between asking for a thing and asking for an action.
bekal: ask what's available and ask for the bill
say what food you like and don't like

dialogs.title: حِوَار — اَلْغَدَاءُ فِي مَطْعَمٍ شَعْبِيٍّ
dialogs.intro: Lunch at a simple restaurant. The waiter comes over to the table.

lines.speaker: اَلنَّادِل:
lines.baca: ahlan wa sahlan! tafaḍḍaluu. maadhaa turiiduun?
lines.id: Welcome! Please, have a seat. What would you like?

lines.speaker: اَلنَّادِل:
lines.text: عِنْدَنَا دَجَاجٌ مَشْوِيٌّ وَسَمَكٌ وَأَرُزٌّ بِالْخُضَارِ.
lines.baca: 'indanaa dajaajun mashwiyy wa samakun wa aruzzun bil-khuḍaar.
lines.id: We have grilled chicken, fish, and rice with vegetables.
lines.literal: at-us chicken grilled and fish and rice with the-vegetables.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: أُرِيدُ دَجَاجًا مَشْوِيًّا مَعَ أَرُزٍّ، مِنْ فَضْلِكَ.
lines.baca: uriidu dajaajan mashwiyyan ma'a aruzz, min faḍlik.
lines.id: I'd like grilled chicken with rice, please.
lines.literal: I-want chicken grilled with rice, from kindness-your.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.baca: wa anaa uriidu samakan wa salaṭah.
lines.id: And I'd like fish and a salad.
lines.literal: and I I-want fish and salad.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: Orange juice for me, and water for her.
lines.literal: juice orange for-me, and water for-her.

lines.speaker: اَلنَّادِل:
lines.id: Certainly. Would you like anything else?

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: By the way, is the food spicy?

lines.speaker: اَلنَّادِل:
lines.id: A little. If you like, without chili.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: No, I like spicy food. Thanks!

notes: **أُرِيدُ is followed by a noun with a fatha.** أُرِيدُ دَجَاجًا — "I want chicken". The thing wanted is the object of the verb, so it takes tanween fatha. To ask for an **action**, the structure is different: أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَشْرَبَ ("I want to drink") — covered fully in unit 17.

**مِنْ فَضْلِكَ literally means "from your kindness".** It is used exactly like "please" and goes at the end of the sentence. To a woman: مِنْ فَضْلِكِ. To several people: مِنْ فَضْلِكُمْ. An even more polite option: لَوْ سَمَحْتَ ("if you would allow").

**مَشْوِيٌّ — an adjective made from a verb.** The pattern مَفْعُول means "having had something done to it", like English *-ed*: شَوَى (grill) → مَشْوِيّ (grilled), كَتَبَ → مَكْتُوب (written), فَتَحَ → مَفْتُوح (opened), قَلَى → مَقْلِيّ (fried). You'll see this pattern everywhere, including on shop signs.

**دَجَاجًا مَشْوِيًّا — the adjective takes tanween fatha too.** You've known since unit 3 that an adjective agrees with its noun. Now you can see that "agreeing" also means copying its final vowel. The rule is consistent, with no exceptions.
**حَاضِرٌ is a waiter's "right away".** Literally "present". It's the standard reply of staff to a request, roughly "certainly, at once". Equivalents: تَمَامٌ ("all right"), حَالًا ("immediately").

**بِدُونِ means "without".** بِدُونِ سُكَّرٍ (without sugar), بِدُونِ فِلْفِلٍ (without chili), بِدُونِ لَحْمٍ (without meat). The next word always takes a kasra, because بِدُون is a preposition. A lifesaver if you have dietary restrictions.

**هَلِ الطَّعَامُ — another kasra.** هَلْ ends in a sukun, and اَلْ also starts with a vowelless letter, so هَلْ becomes هَلِ. You've seen the same thing with مِنَ and كَمِ. One rule: two vowelless letters may not collide.
**اَلطَّعَامَ الْحَارَّ — both take اَلْ.** Since the food is definite, its adjective must be definite as well. Compare طَعَامٌ حَارٌّ ("spicy food", not any particular food).
**بِالْمُنَاسَبَةِ** means "by the way" — a polite way to change the subject, very useful when you want to ask something unrelated to what came before.

grammars.title: Asking politely
body: Arabic has a clear ladder of politeness, and choosing the right rung matters more than choosing the right word.

head: Arabic
Pronunciation
Meaning
Tone
rows: Excuse me / if you don't mind

after: When in doubt, use أُرِيدُ ... مِنْ فَضْلِكَ. It never sounds rude in any situation, and that's worth more than sounding very refined in one situation and awkward in another.
To call the waiter, don't say يَا نَادِل — it sounds like an order. What people actually say: لَوْ سَمَحْتَ ("excuse me") while raising a hand, or in Egypt يَا أُسْطَى.

grammars.title: Saying what you like and don't like
after: Notice that what you like always takes اَلْ: أُحِبُّ الْقَهْوَةَ, not أُحِبُّ قَهْوَةً. Without اَلْ the meaning becomes "I want (a cup of) coffee" — a request, not a statement of taste.
أُحِبُّ is also used for people, and there it fully means "love". For a friend, it's safer to say: هُوَ صَدِيقٌ عَزِيزٌ ("he's a dear friend").

blocks.text: Several of these words reached English long ago by various routes: *sugar* from سُكَّر, *coffee* from قَهْوَة, *syrup* and *sherbet* from شَرَاب, and *candy* from قَنْد. If an English word feels a little exotic yet familiar, there's a good chance it came from Arabic.

blocks.title: Halal, and how to ask about it
items: In Arab countries with a Muslim majority, almost every restaurant is halal and the question rarely needs asking. In Lebanon, Christian areas of Egypt, or international hotel restaurants, it's a normal question: هَلْ هٰذَا حَلَالٌ؟
More often useful: هَلْ فِيهِ لَحْمُ خِنْزِيرٍ؟ ("does it contain pork?") and هَلْ فِيهِ كُحُولٌ؟ ("does it contain alcohol?"). These two questions are specific, so the answers will be specific too.

sections.title: Restaurant phrases, from arriving to leaving

blocks.text: One custom that may differ from home: in many Arab countries the bill is **not** brought until you ask for it. Waiters feel that bringing the bill unasked is like telling guests to leave. So if you've finished and nobody comes, it's not bad service — you're the one who has to say اَلْحِسَابَ، مِنْ فَضْلِكَ.

blocks.title: When you're offered food
items: Offering food again and again is genuine hospitality, not empty formality. A first refusal is often taken as mere politeness, so the host will offer again.

If you're really full: شَبِعْتُ، اَلْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ (*shabi'tu, alhamdulillaah* — "I'm full, thank God"). This is accepted as a sincere and polite refusal, unlike لَا شُكْرًا, which will just get the offer repeated.

vocab.en: excuse me, if you don't mind

answers: أُرِيدُ دَجَاجًا مَشْوِيًّا، مِنْ فَضْلِكَ. — مَاذَا تَشْرَبُ؟ — لَا أُحِبُّ السَّمَكَ. — بِدُونِ سُكَّرٍ، مِنْ فَضْلِكَ. — اَلْحِسَابَ، مِنْ فَضْلِكَ. — اَلطَّعَامُ لَذِيذٌ جِدًّا.
جَوْعَانُ — حَارٌّ — لَذِيذٌ — بِدُونِ — دَوْرَةُ الْمِيَاهِ — اَلْحِسَابَ

Example: أَهْلًا وَسَهْلًا، مَاذَا تُرِيدُ؟ — مَا عِنْدَكُمُ الْيَوْمَ؟ — عِنْدَنَا دَجَاجٌ وَسَمَكٌ. — أُرِيدُ دَجَاجًا مَعَ أَرُزٍّ، مِنْ فَضْلِكَ. — وَعَصِيرَ بُرْتُقَالٍ. — اَلْحِسَابَ، مِنْ فَضْلِكَ.
